\chapter{When, and Then}
\label{ch:hi-when-then}
\hlchaptermodality{72}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask when with kab and set one event against another with the jab/tab frame, hearing each word's job from its first letter.}

Complete HI-R72-when and run all three: ask when the listener can come, say when you feel happiness, and give a reason you cannot come.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kab]{\hi{कब} (\emph{kab}) — when?}

\label{lesson:HI-C72-kab}



\begin{quote}
Run the k- words you now hold: \textbf{\hi{क्या}}, \textbf{\hi{कहाँ}}, \textbf{\hi{क्यों}}, and \emph{kaun}. One question a traveller asks more than any of those is still missing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{कब}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{कब}} — \emph{kab} — \textbf{when?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{कब} \hi{आ} \hi{सकते} \hi{हैं}?} — \emph{āp kab ā sakte haiṁ?} — \textbf{When can you come?}
\end{quote}

Like every Hindi question word, \textbf{\hi{कब}} stays in the sentence's own slot in front of the verb; nothing is fronted and nothing is reordered. Two letters, both of which you can already write.

You have had \textbf{\hi{कल}} since chapter four — \emph{tomorrow}, and also \emph{yesterday}, the same word for both. \textbf{\hi{कब}} is how you ask which day somebody means, and it is the question the whole timetable half of a listening paper is made of.

\textbf{\hi{कब}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{कदा}}, worn down. Its two partners are coming in the next lesson, and they are the same word with different first letters.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āp kab ā sakte haiṁ?}
  \item the same question with \emph{kyoṁ} instead — \emph{āp kyoṁ ā sakte haiṁ?}
  \item the five k- words together — \emph{kyā}, \emph{kaun}, \emph{kahāṁ}, \emph{kyoṁ}, \emph{kab}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{कब}} ask? (\textbf{When}.) Where does it stand? (\textbf{In the sentence's own slot, in front of the verb}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%AC}{Wiktionary: \hi{कब}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jab … tab …]{\hi{जब} … \hi{तब} … (\emph{jab … tab …}) — when, then}

\label{lesson:HI-C72-jab-tab}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the two items before this one by name: \textbf{\hi{क्योंकि}}, and \textbf{\hi{कब}}. Then say the pair the deixis lesson gave you — \textbf{\hi{यह}} and \textbf{\hi{वह}}, \emph{this} and \emph{that}, the \textbf{\hi{य}-} shape and the \textbf{\hi{व}-} shape. That machine is about to run again.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three first letters, one word}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{जब} \hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}, \hi{तब} \hi{आप} \hi{सुनते} \hi{हैं}.} — \emph{jab maiṁ hindī boltā hūṁ, tab āp sunte haiṁ.} — \textbf{When I speak Hindi, then you listen.}
\end{quote}

Look at the three words side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\hi{कब}} & when? — the question \\
\textbf{\hi{जब}} & when — the clause that sets the time \\
\textbf{\hi{तब}} & then — the clause that answers it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One word, three first letters. \textbf{\hi{क}-} asks, \textbf{\hi{ज}-} points back at something, \textbf{\hi{त}-} points at it again. It is exactly the machine the deixis lesson taught with \textbf{\hi{यह}} and \textbf{\hi{वह}}, and Hindi is unusually tidy about it: once you have seen the pattern once you can hear which job a word is doing from its first letter alone.

Hindi says \textbf{both halves}. English drops the \emph{then} and leaves \emph{when I speak Hindi, I feel happiness}; Hindi keeps \textbf{\hi{तब}}, and it earns its place — it is what tells the listener the first clause has finished, which matters far more in a language where every clause ends on a verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kab} · \emph{jab} · \emph{tab}
  \item \emph{jab maiṁ hindī boltā hūṁ, tab āp sunte haiṁ}
  \item which of the three asks a question — \textbf{\hi{कब}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What must follow a \textbf{\hi{जब}} clause? (\textbf{\hi{तब}}.) What do the three first letters do? (\textbf{\hi{क}- asks, \hi{ज}- sets the time, \hi{त}- answers it}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%9C\%E0\%A4\%AC}{Wiktionary: \hi{जब}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kab · jab · tab]{One letter tells you the job}

\label{lesson:HI-R72-when}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{कब}}, \textbf{\hi{जब}}, \textbf{\hi{तब}}. Then say what each first letter does, and name the other pair in the book built the same way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āp kab ā sakte haiṁ?}
  \item \emph{jab maiṁ hindī boltā hūṁ, tab āp sunte haiṁ}
  \item \emph{kyoṁ?} and answer it with \emph{kyoṁki …}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three is a question? (\textbf{\hi{कब}}.) Which two come as a pair in one sentence? (\textbf{\hi{जब} and \hi{तब}}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
